title: Microcallback Stream Adaptor SDK Guidelines (PRD)
content:
Purpose:
This PRD proposes a lightweight streaming adaptor pattern — "microcallback frames" — to standardize low-latency, incremental tool-calling and structured-output ergonomics exposed by Redwood’s Hosted API SDKs. The goal is a minimal, language-agnostic framing and SDK surface that: reduces round trips for tool-heavy flows, keeps client bundles small for mobile/edge, and makes tool invocation predictable and idempotent in partial/streamed responses.

Problem statement:
- Customers building interactive assistants frequently need to interleave model-generated text with precise tool invocations (search, DB write, API call). Existing patterns either: (a) buffer until final output (introduces latency), or (b) stream opaque tokens and rely on client heuristics to extract intent (fragile).
- SDKs often ship heavy runtime logic to handle tool handshake, retry, and resume semantics; this increases mobile bundle size and multiplies failure modes.
- We need a single compatible protocol that works with progressive streaming output, preserves developer ergonomics, and can be rolled out safely alongside current streaming frames.

High-level design idea (microcallback frames):
- Stream payload is divided into small typed frames. Most frames are text deltas; a small set of frames are specialized microcallback frames that signal a tool intent and carry a compact, typed payload.
- Microcallback frame shape (wire): {frame_type: "microcallback", id: string, intent: string, payload: base64(json-inline-or-compact), can_rerun: boolean, resume_token?: string} — SDKs parse this and surface a typed callback to application code.
- Key constraints: frames must be <= 1KB by default; payloads should prefer compact JSON (no large arrays), and binary blobs must be referenced by URL/ID.

Developer ergonomics goals:
- One minimal SDK API across languages: subscribe(stream) -> event callbacks (onText, onMicrocallback, onError, onResume).
- Default runtime should be zero-dependency for JS mobile (no protobufs), tiny parsing logic (~200 LOC).
- Clear idempotency contract: microcallback.id is stable for the session; if the client retries, can_rerun indicates whether server accepts duplicate execution.

Example flow (JS pseudo):
const stream = client.stream({model: 'rwd-rt-small', prompt});
stream.onText(chunk => render(chunk));
stream.onMicrocallback(cb => {
  if (cb.intent === 'search') {
    const q = cb.payload.q;
    // app does the search and returns result to server with stream.signalCallbackResult(cb.id, {hits})
  }
});

Server expectations:
- Server emits microcallback frames only at stable phrase boundaries (avoid mid-token splits).
- Server must expose a companion endpoint /v1/streams/{stream_id}/callbacks/{id}/response to receive callback results. This endpoint is idempotent and accepts a well-formed JSON result.
- Optionally support direct signed upload URLs if callback results include larger artifacts (images, logs).

Resume and offline semantics:
- Streams may be resumed using resume_token frames. SDK should provide a resume() helper that replays the local state and requests server to continue from resume_token.
- For mobile/spotty networks, SDK can persist pending microcallback items and synchronize when connectivity resumes. The wire id + can_rerun flag guide safe execution.

Fallbacks and graceful degradation:
- If client cannot deliver callback result within TTL, server may continue with a lightweight fallback intent (e.g., skip to best-effort answer) and emit a fallback_hint frame.
- SDK-level policy: configurable timeouts, automatic fallback to local heuristics, and an opt-in offlineQueuedCallbacks mode.

Structured output compatibility:
- Microcallback frames are complementary to typed structured output frames. If the model emits a final structured object, it can reference callback ids to indicate which external data populated fields.
- Example: final object {summary: '...', sources: [{callback_id: 'cb-123', field: 'results'}]} allows auditing and traceability in Console.

Telemetry and observability:
- New telemetry events: microcallback.emitted, microcallback.delivered (client->server), microcallback.executed, microcallback.timedout, microcallback.fallbacked.
- Payload sizes and rates tracked per model and per route to tune default frame size limit.
- Console: show callback timeline in request trace with links to callback result artifacts and client-side logs (if client uploads).

SDK surfaces (proposal):
- Core API (all SDKs): StreamClient.stream(params) returns StreamHandle with: onText, onMicrocallback, onError, onClose, resume(token), signalCallbackResult(id, result).
- Tiny helper libs: validation helpers for compact JSON payloads, optional serializer to compress payload fields for low-bandwidth clients.
- Secure helpers: signed-url helper for uploading artifacts returned by callbacks.

Safety and security:
- Callback ops that mutate customer data must require an explicit capability (token scope) and be logged.
- Callbacks that trigger outbound network calls from the app should be explicit and have an allowed-hosts policy.

Rollout plan (staged):
1) Internal alpha with eng + SE customers: instrument microcallback.emitted telemetry, allow a feature flag on routes. (2 months)
2) Beta with limited customer opt-in and console tracing for callbacks. SDK stable JS + Python lightweight implementations. (2 months)
3) GA: enable opt-out default for new streaming routes and publish SDKs for major languages plus migration docs. (2 months)

Metrics / success criteria:
- Developer time: reduce average integration time for tool flows by 30% vs current best-effort patterns.
- Latency: reduce perceived tool-call latency (time to first action result) by 20% for interactive flows that adopt microcallbacks.
- Error surface: decrease client-side parsing errors for tool dispatch by 50% when using SDKs.
- Adoption: 15% of new streaming routes adopt microcallback within 6 months of GA.

Compatibility and interactions with existing features:
- Backwards compatible: existing clients that ignore microcallback frames should continue to render text; server should include short human-readable text around callbacks to avoid confusing end users.
- Interoperate with our existing structured output frames and resumable sessions; mapping rules defined in Appendix A (linked doc).

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- Frame size limit: 1KB default vs 4KB tradeoff for more expressive payloads at cost of mobile bandwidth. Need telemetry pilot.
- Idempotency enforcement: who enforces uniqueness of callback IDs across resumed sessions? Propose stream-scoped uniqueness; evaluate cross-stream uniqueness later.
- How much of the callback lifecycle should SDKs automanage vs leave to application code? Minimalist approach recommended initially.

Acceptance criteria (for GA):
- SDKs in JS and Python implement StreamHandle API and pass compatibility tests.
- Server emits microcallback frames under feature-flag and supports callback result endpoint with idempotent semantics.
- Console traces show callback events and can link to uploaded artifacts.
- Run end-to-end integration with two pilot customers (one mobile-first, one SaaS assistant).

Risks and mitigations:
- Increased attack surface if callback payloads cause unsafe client behavior -> strict payload validation and scoped tokens.
- Client fragmentation (different SDK behaviors) -> provide canonical conformance test and tiny reference implementations.

Next steps:
- Implementation spike: JS SDK minimal parser + server emission (2 weeks).
- Telemetry schema: draft by observability team (1 week).
- Pilot with Solutions Eng and one early customer (4 weeks).

Appendix: brief sample frames (wire-friendly compact form)
- text frame: {t:'T', d:'delta text'}
- microcallback frame: {t:'C', id:'cb-0001', i:'search', p:'{q:\"redwood inference\"}', r:true}
- resume frame: {t:'R', token:'s-xyz'}

Notes to reviewers:
- Focus feedback on SDK ergonomics and security scopes.
- If you think microcallback should be combined with our existing structured-frame proposal, explain the concrete developer UX gains or losses.
